nodes.label: Calculate area using formulae
nodes.description: Calculate the area of a square, rectangle, triangle, trapezium, parallelogram or circle by choosing the correct area formula, including finding a missing height with the Pythagoras theorem first.

nodes.label: Surface area of right prisms
nodes.description: Calculate the surface area of a right prism (rectangular or triangular) by sketching its net, finding the area of each face and adding the areas together.

nodes.label: Surface area of a cylinder
nodes.description: Calculate the surface area of a cylinder as the area of its two circular ends plus the curved surface, which unfolds into a rectangle whose length is the circumference of the base.

nodes.label: Volume of right prisms
nodes.description: Calculate the volume of a right prism (cube, rectangular prism or triangular prism) by finding the area of its base and multiplying it by its height, giving the answer in cubic units

nodes.label: Volume of a cylinder
nodes.description: Calculate the volume of a cylinder, correct to a given number of decimal places, as the area of its circular base multiplied by its height

nodes.label: Surface area of pyramids
nodes.description: Calculate the total surface area of a right square pyramid or triangular pyramid as the area of the base plus the area of the triangular sides, using the theorem of Pythagoras where a height has to be found.

nodes.label: Surface area of a cone
nodes.description: Calculate the total surface area of a right cone as the area of the circular base plus the area of the walls, using the slant height (found with the theorem of Pythagoras where it is not given), and show how the cone's surface area formula is obtained.

nodes.label: Surface area of a sphere
nodes.description: Calculate the surface area of a sphere from its radius using $4\pi{r}^{2}$, correct to the required number of decimal places.

nodes.label: Volume of pyramids, cones, spheres
nodes.description: Calculate the volume of a square pyramid, triangular pyramid, right cone or sphere by substituting the given dimensions into the volume formula, including finding the base area or pyramid height first where needed.

nodes.label: Composite solids: volume and surface area
nodes.description: Calculate the volume and the total surface area of a composite solid made of a pyramid on a prism or cube, adding the volumes and the areas of the exposed faces of its parts.

nodes.label: Surface area of pyramids, cones
nodes.description: Calculate the surface area of a right pyramid or right cone from its base dimensions and slant height.

nodes.label: Scaling a rectangular prism
nodes.description: Calculate the new surface area and volume of a rectangular prism when one, two or all three of its dimensions are multiplied by a constant factor, and express each as a factor of the original.

nodes.label: Effect of scaling one dimension
nodes.description: Derive, in terms of k, the new volume and surface area of a prism or cylinder when one of its dimensions is multiplied by a constant factor k.

nodes.label: Apply scale factor rules
nodes.description: Determine the new area, surface area or volume of a shape or solid when all of its dimensions are multiplied by a constant factor, using the relationships that area scales by k^2 and volume by k^3.

questions.stem: If a litre of paint covers an area of $\text{2}$ $\text{m}^{2}$ , how much paint does a painter need to cover: a rectangular swimming pool with dimensions $\text{4}\text{m}\times\text{3}\text{m}\times\text{2.5}\text{m}$ (the inside walls and floor only);
solution: We need to find the surface area of the pool. In this case we have a rectangular prism but with one rectangle missing (which would be the top of the pool).

$\begin{aligned}\text{surface area}&=\text{area of bottom of pool}+2(\text{area of long sides})\\&+2(\text{area of short sides})\\&=(\text{4}\times\text{3})+2(\text{4}\times\text{2.5})+2(\text{3}\times\text{2.5})\\&=\text{12}+\text{20}+\text{15}\\&=\text{47}\text{ m}^{2}\end{aligned}$

The painter needs one litre of paint for every $\text{2}$ $\text{m}^{2}$ of area. So we must divide the surface area by 2 to find the total amount of paint needed. Therefore, the painter will need $\frac{47}{2}=\text{24}\text{ l}$ of paint (rounded up to the nearest litre).

questions.stem: If a litre of paint covers an area of $\text{2}$ $\text{m}^{2}$ , how much paint does a painter need to cover: the inside walls and floor of a circular reservoir with diameter $\text{4}$ $\text{m}$ and height $\text{2.5}$ $\text{m}$ . [figure]
solution: We need to find the surface area of the reservoir. In this case we have a cylinder but with one circle missing (which would be the top of the reservoir). We are given the diameter of the reservoir. The radius is half the diameter and so $r=\text{2}\text{m}$ .

$\begin{aligned}\text{surface area}&=\text{area of bottom of reservoir}+\text{area of inside of reservoir}\\&=(\pi r^{2})+(\text{circumference of base}\times\text{height of reservoir})\\&=(\pi(\text{2})^{2})+(2(\pi)(\text{2})\times\text{2.5})\\&=14\pi\\&\approx\text{44}\text{ m}^{2}\end{aligned}$

The painter needs one litre of paint for every $\text{2}$ $\text{m}^{2}$ of area. So we must divide the surface area by 2 to find the total amount of paint needed. Therefore, the painter will need $\frac{44}{2}=\text{22}\text{ l}$ of paint (rounded up to the nearest litre).

questions.stem: The figure here is a triangular prism. The height of the prism is $\text{12}$ units; the triangles, which are both right triangles, have sides which are $\text{5}$ , $\text{12}$ and $\text{13}$ units long. Find the surface area of the figure. [figure]
solution: A triangular prism is made up of 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. In this case the triangles are right-angled triangles and so we have the height of the triangle. We also note that each rectangle has a different length and breadth.

$\begin{aligned}A_{\triangle\text{ prism}}&=2A_{\text{triangles}}+3A_{\text{rectangles}}\\&=2\left[\frac{1}{2}b_{\triangle}h_{\triangle}\right]+b_{1}h_{1}+b_{2}h_{2}+b_{3}h_{3}\\&=2\left[\frac{1}{2}(\text{5})(\text{12})\right]+(\text{12})(\text{12})+(\text{5})(\text{12})+(\text{13})(\text{12})\\&=\text{60}+\text{144}+\text{60}+\text{156}\\&=\text{420}\end{aligned}$

questions.stem: The figure here is a rectangular prism. The height of the prism is $\text{5}$ units; the other dimensions of the prism are $\text{8}$ and $\text{5}$ units. Find the surface area of the figure. [figure]
solution: A rectangular prism is made up of 6 rectangles. In this case there are 4 rectangles with a breadth of 5 units and a height of 8 units and two rectangles with a breadth of 5 units and a height of 5 units.

$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{rectangular prism}}&=A_{\text{6 rectangles}}\\&=4(b_{1}h_{1})+2(b_{2}h_{2})\\&=4(\text{8})(\text{5})+2(\text{5})(\text{5})\\&=4(\text{40})+2(\text{25})\\&=\text{210}\end{aligned}$

questions.stem: A triangular pyramid is placed on top of a triangular prism, as shown below. The base of the prism is an equilateral triangle of side length $\text{20}$ $\text{cm}$ and the height of the prism is $\text{42}$ $\text{cm}$ . The pyramid has a height of $\text{12}$ $\text{cm}$ . Calculate the total volume of the object. [figure]
solution: Calculate the volume of the prism: First find the height of the base triangle using the theorem of Pythagoras: [figure] Next find the area of the base triangle: $\begin{aligned}\text{areaofbasetriangle}&=\frac{1}{2}\times20\times10\sqrt{3}\\&=100\sqrt{3}~\text{cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$ Now we can find the volume of the prism: $\begin{aligned}\therefore\text{volume of prism}&=\text{area of base triangle}\times\text{height of prism}\\&=\text{100}\sqrt{\text{3}}\times\text{42}\\&=\text{4200}\sqrt{\text{3}}\text{ cm}^{3}\end{aligned}$

Calculate the volume of the pyramid: The area of the base triangle is equal to the area of the base of the pyramid. $\begin{aligned}\therefore\text{volume of pyramid}&=\frac{1}{3}\left(\text{area of base}\right)\times H\\&=\frac{1}{3}\times100\sqrt{3}\times12\\&=400\sqrt{3}~\text{cm}^{3}\end{aligned}$

Calculate the total volume: $\begin{aligned}\text{total volume}&=\text{4200}\sqrt{\text{3}}+\text{400}\sqrt{\text{3}}\\&=\text{4600}\sqrt{\text{3}}\\&=\text{7967.4}\text{ cm}^{3}\end{aligned}$ Therefore the total volume of the object is $\text{7967.4}$ $\text{cm}^{3}$ .

questions.stem: With the same complex object as in the previous example, you are given the additional information that the slant height ${h}_{s}$ = $\text{13.3}$ $\text{cm}$ . Now calculate the total surface area of the object.

Calculate the total surface area of the object: $\begin{aligned}\text{total surface area}&=\text{area of base of prism}+\text{area of sides of prism}+\text{area of exposed faces of pyramid}\\&=\left(\text{100}\sqrt{\text{3}}\right)+\text{3}\left(\text{840}\right)+\text{3}\left(\text{133}\right)\\&=\text{3092.2}\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$ Therefore the total surface area (of the exposed faces) of the object is $\text{3092.2}$ $\text{cm}^{2}$ .

questions.stem: If the length of the radius of a circle is a third of its original size, what will the area of the new circle be? [figure]
solution: The area of the original circle is: $\pi r^{2}$ . Now we reduce the radius by a third. In other words we multiply $r$ by one third. The new area is:
$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{new}}&=\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}r\right)^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{9}\pi r^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{9}A\end{aligned}$
Therefore, if the radius of a circle is a third of its original size, the area of the new circle will be $\frac{1}{9}$ the original area.

questions.stem: If the length of the base's radius and height of a cone is doubled, what will the surface area of the new cone be? [figure]
solution: We can find the new area by noting that the area will change by a factor of $k$ when we change the dimensions of the cone. In this case we are changing two dimensions of the cone and so the new area will be: $A_{\text{new}}=k^{2}A$ The value of $k$ comes from the word “doubled” in the question: the value of $k$ is 2. So the new area of the cone will be $A_{\text{new}}=4\times A$ if we double the height and the base's radius of the cone. Therefore the surface area of the new cone will be 4 times the original surface area.

questions.stem: Describe the change in the volume of a rectangular prism if the: length and breadth increase by a constant factor of $\text{3}$ .
solution: The volume of a rectangular prism is given by $V=l\times b\times h$ . If we increase the length and breadth by a constant factor of 3 the volume is:
$\begin{aligned}V_{\text{new}}&=3(l)\times3(b)\times h\\&=9V\end{aligned}$
Therefore the volume of the prism increases by a factor of 9 when the length and breadth are increased by a constant factor of 3.

questions.stem: Describe the change in the volume of a rectangular prism if the: length, breadth and height are multiplied by a constant factor of $\text{3}$ .
solution: The volume of a rectangular prism is given by $V=l\times b\times h$ . If we increase the length, breadth and height by a constant factor of 3 the volume is:
$\begin{aligned}V_{\text{new}}&=3(l)\times3(b)\times3(h)\\&=27V\end{aligned}$
Therefore the volume of the prism increases by a factor of 27 when the length, breadth and height are increased by a constant factor of 3.

Therefore, if each side of a triangular prism is quadrupled, the volume of the new triangular prism will be 64 times the original shape's volume.

questions.stem: If the length of each side of a square is a quarter of its original size, what will the area of the new square be?
solution: When we multiply the sides of a square by a factor of $k$ the area of the square will increase by $k^{2}$ . In this case we are making each side of the square a quarter of the original size so we get:
$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{new}}&=\left(\frac{1}{4}s\right)^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{16}s^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{16}A\end{aligned}$
Therefore, if each side of a square is a quarter of its original size, the area of the new square will be $\frac{1}{16}$ times the original square's area.

questions.stem: If the length of each side of a square pyramid is a third of its original size, what will the surface area of the new square pyramid be?

Therefore, if each side of a square pyramid is a third of its original size, the surface area of the new square pyramid will be $\frac{1}{9}$ times the original shape's surface area.

questions.stem: If the length of the base's radius and the height of a cylinder is halved, what will the volume of the new cylinder be?
solution: In this case the base's radius and the height of a cylinder is half of the original size so we get:
$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{new}}&=\frac{1}{3}\pi\left(\frac{1}{2}r\right)^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}H\right)\\&=\frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}H\right)\\&=\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}$
Therefore, if the base's radius and the height of a cylinder is halved, the volume of the new cylinder will be $\frac{1}{8}$ times the original shape's volume.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Volume}&=\text{volume of cube}+\text{volume of square pyramid}\\&=s^{3}+\frac{1}{3}bH\\&=(\text{5})^{3}+\frac{1}{3}(\text{5})^{2}(\text{6})\\&=\text{175}\text{ cm}^{3}\end{aligned}$

For the surface area we note that one face of the cube is covered by the pyramid. We also note that the base of the pyramid is covered by the cube. So we only need to find the area of 5 sides of the cube and the four triangular faces of the pyramid. For the triangular faces we need the slant height. We can calculate this using the theorem of Pythagoras:
$\begin{aligned}h_{s}^{2}&=H^{2}+\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^{2}\\&=(6)^{2}+(\text{2.5})^{2}\\h_{s}&=\sqrt{\text{42.25}}\end{aligned}$

The surface area is $\text{190}$ $\text{cm}^{2}$ and the volume is $\text{175}$ $\text{cm}^{3}$ .

Consider a rectangular prism with a height of $\text{4}$ $\text{cm}$ and base lengths of $\text{3}$ $\text{cm}$ . [figure] Calculate the surface area and volume. Express the new surface area and volume as a factor of the original surface area and volume.

Calculate the original volume and surface area: $\begin{aligned}V&=l\times b\times h\\&=3\times3\times4\\&=36\text{cm}^{3}\\\\A&=2\left[(l\times h)+(l\times b)+(b\times h)\right]\\&=2\left[(3\times4)+(3\times3)+(3\times4)\right]\\&=66\text{cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

Calculate the new volume and surface area: Two of the dimensions are multiplied by a factor of 3. $\begin{aligned}V_{n}&=3l\times3b\times h\\&=3(3)\times3(3)\times4\\&=324\text{cm}^{3}\\\\A_{n}&=2\left[(3l\times h)+(3l\times3b)+(3b\times h)\right]\\&=2\left[(3(3)\times4)+(3(3)\times3(3))+(3(3)\times4)\right]\\&=306\text{cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

Express the new dimensions as a factor of the original dimensions: $\begin{aligned}V&=36\\{V}_{n}&=324\\\frac{{V}_{n}}{V}&=\frac{324}{36}\\&=9\\\therefore{V}_{n}&=9V\\&={3}^{2}V\\\\A&=66\\{A}_{n}&=306\\\frac{{A}_{n}}{A}&=\frac{306}{66}\\\therefore{A}_{n}&=\frac{306}{66}A\\&=\frac{51}{11}A\end{aligned}$
Prove that if the height of a rectangular prism with dimensions $l$ , $b$ and $h$ is multiplied by a constant value of $k$ , the volume will also increase by a factor $k$ . [figure]

Calculate the new volume: The new dimensions are $l$ , $b$ , and $kh$ and so the new volume is: $\begin{aligned}{V}_{n}&=l\times b\times\left(kh\right)\\&=k\left(lbh\right)\\&=kV\end{aligned}$
Write the final answer: If the height of a rectangular prism is multiplied by a constant $k$ , then the volume also increases by a factor of $k$ .

Consider a cylinder with a radius of $r$ and a height of $h$ . Calculate the new volume and surface area (expressed in terms of $r$ and $h$ ) if the radius is multiplied by a constant factor of $k$ . [figure]

claims.claim: Area is the two dimensional space inside the boundary of a flat object.
Area is measured in square units.
The area of a square is A = s^2, where s is the side length.
The area of a rectangle is A = b × h.
The area of a triangle is A = 1/2 b × h.
The area of a trapezium is A = 1/2 (a + b) × h.
The area of a parallelogram is A = b × h.
The area of a circle is A = πr^2.
The circumference of a circle is 2πr.

A triangular prism has a triangle as its base.
A rectangular prism has a rectangle as its base.

Volume is the three dimensional space occupied by an object, or the contents of an object.
Volume is measured in cubic units.
The volume of a right prism is calculated by multiplying the area of the base of the solid by the height of the solid.
The volume of a cylinder is calculated by multiplying the area of the base of the solid by the height of the solid.
For a rectangular prism, the base is a rectangle, so volume = area of base × height = area of rectangle × height = l × b × h.

A pyramid is a geometric solid that has a polygon as its base and faces that converge at a point called the apex.
In a pyramid the faces are not perpendicular to the base.
The triangular pyramid and the square pyramid take their names from the shape of their base.
A pyramid is called a right pyramid if the line between the apex and the centre of the base is perpendicular to the base.
The surface area of a square pyramid is the area of the base plus the area of the triangular sides.
For a square pyramid, surface area = b² + 4(½ b h_s), where b² is the area of the base and each of the 4 triangular sides has area ½ b h_s.

When one or more of the dimensions of a prism or cylinder is multiplied by a constant, its surface area and volume change.
The new surface area and volume of a prism or cylinder whose dimensions have been multiplied by a constant are calculated by using the surface area and volume formulae from the preceding section.
There is a relationship between the change in dimensions and the resulting change in surface area and volume.
These relationships are used to calculate the new volume or surface area of an object more simply when its dimensions are scaled up or down.
The dimensions of a rectangular prism are written l, b and h.
To see the effect of scaling, multiply one, two and then three of the dimensions of the rectangular prism by a constant factor (here 5) and calculate the new volume and surface area each time.
The volume of a rectangular prism with dimensions l, b and h is V = l × b × h = lbh.
The surface area of a rectangular prism with dimensions l, b and h is A = 2[(l × h) + (l × b) + (b × h)] = 2(lh + lb + bh).
When one dimension of a rectangular prism (the height) is multiplied by 5, the new volume is V1 = l × b × 5h = 5(lbh) = 5V.
When one dimension of a rectangular prism (the height) is multiplied by 5, the new surface area is A1 = 2[(l × 5h) + (l × b) + (b × 5h)] = 2(5lh + lb + 5bh).
When two dimensions of a rectangular prism (l and h) are multiplied by 5, the new volume is V2 = 5l × b × 5h = 5.5(lbh) = 5^2 × V.
When two dimensions of a rectangular prism (l and h) are multiplied by 5, the new surface area is A2 = 2[(5l × 5h) + (5l × b) + (b × 5h)] = 2 × 5(5lh + lb + bh).

When all three dimensions of a rectangular prism are multiplied by 5, the new surface area is A3 = 2(5^2 lh + 5^2 lb + 5^2 bh) = 5^2 × 2(lh + lb + bh) = 5^2 A.
When all three dimensions of a rectangular prism are multiplied by a factor k, the new volume is V_k = kl × kb × kh = k^3(lbh) = k^3 V; volume is multiplied by k^3.

When all three dimensions of a rectangular prism are multiplied by a factor k, the new surface area is A_k = 2[(kl × kh) + (kl × kb) + (kb × kh)] = k^2 × 2(lh + lb + bh) = k^2 A; surface area is multiplied by k^2.
The new surface area is written A_n and the new volume is written V_n.
